'''Alan Hugh Schoen''' (December 11, 1924 – July 26, 2023) was an American physicist and computer scientist best known for his discovery of the [[gyroid]], an infinitely connected triply periodic [[minimal surface]].

==Professional career==
Alan Schoen received his B.S. degree in physics from [[Yale University]] in 1945, followed by his M.S. and Ph.D. in physics from [[University of Illinois]] at Urbana-Champaign in 1951 and 1958, respectively.<ref name="thesis"/> His doctoral dissertation was entitled “Self-Diffusion in Alpha Solid Solutions of Silver-Cadmium and Silver-Indium.”<ref name="thesis">{{Cite thesis |title=Self-Diffusion in Alpha Solid Solutions of Silver-Cadmium and Silver-Indium |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2142/76317 |publisher=University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign |date=1958 |degree=text |first=Alan Hugh |last=Schoen|hdl=2142/76317 }}</ref> After completing graduate work he was employed (between 1957 and 1967) as a research physicist by aerospace companies in California, and also worked as a free-lance solid-state physics consultant. In 1967, he took the position of senior scientist at [[NASA]]'s Electronics Research Center (ERC) in Cambridge, Massachusetts,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Alan Schoen geometry |url=https://schoengeometry.com/e-tpms.html |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=schoengeometry.com}}</ref> where he did geometry research and served as the Chief of the Office of Geometrical Applications.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}} While at NASA, he also worked on expandable space frames.<ref>NASA Tech Brief. January 1975. https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19740000252.pdf</ref> In 1970, Schoen accepted a position at [[California Institute of the Arts]], where he taught calculus and computer graphics. In 1973, he accepted a teaching position in the Department of Design at [[Southern Illinois University Carbondale]] (SIUC),<ref>{{Cite web |title=People - SIU - Department of Design |url=https://siudesign.org/people.htm |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=siudesign.org}}</ref> where he taught computer graphics, algebra, and analytic geometry to design students. This was a former home department of [[Buckminster Fuller]] - an American designer and inventor who popularized the [[geodesic dome]]. In 1982, Schoen accepted a joint appointment in the Department of Mathematics and Department of Computer Science at SIUC. In August 1985, he moved to the SIUC campus in Nakajo, Japan, where he taught a course in computer science and also helped to teach English at a local Japanese junior high school.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}} Upon his return to Carbondale in 1988, he taught [[Fortran|FORTRAN]] and Digital Design in the Electrical Engineering Department at SIUC until his retirement in 1995.

After retiring from academia he continued his work on numerous infinite families of minimal surfaces and on inventing geometric puzzles and images.<ref>SIU Dept. of Mathematics. Alan Schoen - Gyroid. http://math.siu.edu/faculty-staff/about-us/gyroid.php {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171029012854/http://math.siu.edu/faculty-staff/about-us/gyroid.php |date=2017-10-29 }}</ref> He was active in the early days of the recreational math conference called [[Gathering 4 Gardner]].
{{clear}}

==Contributions==
[[File:Gyroid unit cell stereo image.jpg|thumb|upright=2.2|Stereo image of gyroid unit cell by Alan Schoen (2014)]]
Alan Schoen is best known for discovering (while working at NASA) a minimal surface that he named the [[gyroid]].<ref name="Schoen1970">Schoen, Alan H. (1970). "Infinite periodic minimal surfaces without self-intersections." https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19700020472_1970020472.pdf {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527060728/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19700020472_1970020472.pdf |date=May 27, 2010}}</ref><ref>Schoen, A.H.: Infinite Regular Warped Polyhedra and Infinite Periodic Minimal Surfaces. ''Not. Amer. Math. Soc.'', vol. 15, 1968, p. 727.</ref><ref>Schoen, A.H.: A Fifth Intersection-Free Infinite Periodic Minimal Surface of Cubic Symmetry. ''Not. Amer. Math. Soc.'', vol. 16, 1969, p. 519.</ref> The name stems from the impression in the gyroid's structure that each continuous channel in the array, along different principal crystallographic axes, has connections to additional intersecting channels, which “gyrate” along the channel length.<ref>James A. Dolan, Bodo D. Wilts, [[Silvia Vignolini]], Jeremy J. Baumberg, Ullrich Steiner, and Timothy D. Wilkinson. Optical Properties of Gyroid Structured Materials: From Photonic Crystals to Metamaterials. ''Adv. Optical Mater.'' 2014, DOI: 10.1002/adom.201400333 https://www.np.phy.cam.ac.uk/uploads/2014-uploads/AdvOptMat14_gyroidreview.pdf</ref> The gyroid has become popular among scientists as more and more new occurrences of it in nature are being discovered.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home {{!}} Cornell Chronicle |url=https://news.cornell.edu/ |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=news.cornell.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=week225 |url=https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/week225.html |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=math.ucr.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Keim |first=Brandon |title=Butterfly Wing Colors Come From Space-Age Structures |language=en-US |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2010/06/butterfly-colors/ |access-date=2023-08-11 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref>
Earlier in his career, while conducting his doctoral research on [[atomic diffusion]] in solids (1957), Schoen discovered that for self-diffusion in crystalline solids, there is a simple relation between the Bardeen-Hering correlation factor and the isotope effect that makes it possible to distinguish between ''vacancy'' and ''interstitial'' diffusion mechanisms. He later found evidence from a FORTRAN program that his equation is exact in all close-packed cubic structures.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physical Review Letters - Volume 1 Issue 4 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/issues/1/4 |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=journals.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> His finding was soon confirmed algebraically by Tharmalingam and Lidiard.<ref>K. Tharmalingam and A.B. Lidiard. Isotope effect in vacancy diffusion. ''The Philosophical Magazine'' Series 8, Volume 4, 1959 - Issue 44. http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/14786435908238264?needAccess=true&journalCode=tphm19&</ref> Schoen's preoccupation with this subject eventually led him to an interest in minimal surfaces and the discovery of the gyroid.<ref name=":0"/>

Schoen also published scientific papers on families of minimal surfaces, and books on geometric images and puzzles.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kadon Enterprises, Inc., Alan Schoen profile |url=http://www.gamepuzzles.com/schoen.htm |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=www.gamepuzzles.com}}</ref> In the early 1990s, Schoen designed Rombix<ref>Rombix. Illustrated Booklet. http://schoengeometry.com/b-fintil-media/little_red_book.pdf</ref> — a combinatorial dissection puzzle, which uses multicolored tiles that are composites of 8-zonogons, to create various designs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=isbn:9810247028 - Google Search |url=https://www.google.com/search?tbm=bks&q=isbn:9810247028 |access-date=2023-08-11 |website=www.google.com}}</ref> He also developed The Geometry Garret, a website full of different families of geometric structures (considered "cool stuff" by Alan's academic colleagues).<ref name=":0" /><ref>Alan Schoen. Infiite Tilings. http://schoengeometry.com/c-infintil.html</ref> Alan Schoen held U.S. patents (see below) for six of his inventions.

==Death==
Alan Schoen died in [[Carbondale, Illinois]], on July 26, 2023, at the age of 98.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Alan Hugh Schoen |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/name/alan-schoen-obituary?id=52575876 |website=Legacy |access-date=29 July 2023}}</ref>
